description: Reading, building, comparing and rounding numbers

lessons.title: Numbers All Around Us
lessons.intro: From the pages in your book to the runs in a cricket match, numbers are everywhere. Big numbers are just small numbers joined together in a clever way!
explanation: A number is made of digits (0-9). Where a digit sits decides how much it is worth.
We read numbers from left to right, grouping into thousands, hundreds, tens and ones.
For example, 4,206 is read 'four thousand two hundred six'.
lessons.rule: Every digit has a value that depends on its position.
lessons.tip: Read big numbers left to right, one group at a time.

lessons.title: Digits and Positions
lessons.intro: The same digit can mean very different things. The 5 in 500 is much bigger than the 5 in 5!
explanation: A 4-digit number has places for ones, tens, hundreds and thousands.
In 3,742 the digit 3 is in the thousands place, so it means 3,000.
Reading the position carefully is the first step to understanding any number.
lessons.rule: Position tells you a digit's true size.
lessons.tip: Always find the ones place first, then count left.

lessons.title: Writing Numbers in Figures
lessons.intro: When someone says a number out loud, you can write it in figures by listening for 'thousand', 'hundred', and so on.
explanation: 'Seven thousand ninety' becomes 7,090 — notice the 0 holding the hundreds place.
Zeros are important place-holders; they keep the other digits in the correct spot.
Without the 0, 7,090 would wrongly become 790.
lessons.rule: Use 0 to hold any empty place.
lessons.tip: Say the number slowly and write one group at a time.

lessons.title: How Many Digits?
lessons.intro: Counting digits helps you know how big a number is. More digits usually means a bigger number!
explanation: The largest 3-digit number is 999; the smallest 4-digit number is 1,000.
Adding 1 to 999 makes 1,000 — a brand new thousands place appears.
The largest 4-digit number is 9,999.
lessons.rule: Each new place lets numbers grow ten times bigger.
lessons.tip: If two numbers have different digit counts, the longer one is larger.

lessons.title: Making Numbers from Digits
lessons.intro: Give me some digits and I can build the biggest or smallest number by arranging them cleverly.
explanation: To make the biggest number, put the largest digits on the left.
To make the smallest, put the smallest digits on the left — but never a 0 at the very front.
With 3, 9, 1, 7 the biggest 4-digit number is 9,731.
lessons.rule: Biggest number: large digits first. Smallest: small digits first (no leading 0).
lessons.tip: Sort the digits first, then place them.

quiz.question: Write in figures: four thousand two hundred six.
quiz.hint: Four groups: 4 thousands, 2 hundreds, 0 tens, 6 ones.

quiz.question: Write in figures: seven thousand ninety.
quiz.hint: Ninety is 9 tens; there are no hundreds, so use 0.

quiz.question: How many digits are there in the number 10,000?
What is the largest 3-digit number?
quiz.hint: All three places hold the biggest digit, 9.

quiz.question: A stadium has fifty-two thousand seats. Write this number in figures.
quiz.hint: Fifty-two thousand = 52 followed by three zeros.
quiz.story: The new cricket stadium is huge!

quiz.question: Ravi wrote the smallest 4-digit number. What number did he write?
quiz.hint: The smallest 4-digit number starts with 1 and then zeros.

quiz.question: What is the largest 4-digit number using the digits 3, 9, 1, 7 each once?
quiz.hint: Put the biggest digits on the left: 9, then 7, then 3, then 1.

quiz.question: What is the smallest 4-digit number using the digits 4, 0, 6, 2 each once (no leading zero)?
quiz.hint: Smallest non-zero digit goes first, then the 0.

lessons.title: Place Value vs Face Value
lessons.intro: Every digit has two values: its face value (the digit itself) and its place value (what it is worth where it sits).
explanation: Face value of 7 in 4,703 is simply 7.
Place value of 7 in 4,703 is 700, because 7 sits in the hundreds place.
Face value never changes; place value depends on position.
lessons.rule: Face value = the digit. Place value = digit x its place.
lessons.tip: Ask: 'Which place?' then multiply.

steps.text: Face value is just the digit you see.
Place value multiplies the digit by its place (ones, tens, hundreds...).
steps.tip: 7 is in the hundreds place here.

lessons.title: The Thousands Place
lessons.intro: When a digit sits in the thousands place, it is worth a whole thousand times itself.
explanation: Place value of 8 in 8,159 is 8,000.
Place value of 3 in 3,642 is 3,000.
The leftmost digit of a 4-digit number is always in the thousands place.
lessons.rule: Thousands place: multiply the digit by 1,000.
lessons.tip: Count places from the right: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands.

lessons.title: The Mighty Zero
lessons.intro: Zero may look empty, but it does a big job — it holds a place so other digits stay put.
explanation: Place value of 0 in 4,082 is 0.
Even though its place value is 0, the 0 keeps the 4 in the thousands place.
Remove the 0 and 4,082 wrongly becomes 482.
lessons.rule: A zero's place value is 0, but it still holds the place.
lessons.tip: Never drop a middle zero when writing numbers.

lessons.title: Comparing the Two Values
lessons.intro: Sometimes a question asks for the difference between place value and face value — a neat little puzzle.
explanation: For 3 in 5,347: place value 300, face value 3.
Their difference is 300 - 3 = 297.
This difference is big when the digit sits far to the left.
lessons.rule: Difference = place value - face value.
lessons.tip: Find both values first, then subtract.

lessons.title: Two of the Same Digit
lessons.intro: What if a number has the same digit twice? Each copy has its own place value!
explanation: In 3,434 there are two 4s: one in the hundreds (400) and one in the ones (4).
Their place values are 400 and 4.
Add them to get 404.
lessons.rule: Each repeated digit keeps its own place value.
lessons.tip: Handle each copy separately, then combine.

quiz.question: What is the place value of 6 in 3,642?
quiz.hint: 6 sits in the hundreds place: 6 x 100.

quiz.question: What is the place value of 8 in 8,159?
quiz.hint: 8 sits in the thousands place: 8 x 1000.

quiz.question: What is the face value of 5 in 7,526?
quiz.hint: Face value is just the digit itself.

quiz.question: What is the place value of 0 in 4,082?
In 5,347, what is the place value of 3 minus its face value?
quiz.hint: Place value is 300, face value is 3.
quiz.story: A number puzzle from Meena's workbook.

quiz.question: In 9,210, what is the place value of 9 minus the place value of 2?
In 3,434, what is the sum of the place values of the two 4s?
quiz.hint: One 4 is in hundreds, the other in ones.

quiz.question: In 6,767, add the place value of 7 in the tens place to the place value of 6 in the thousands place.

lessons.title: Breaking Numbers Apart
lessons.intro: Expanded form shows a number as the sum of its place values — like taking a toy apart to see its pieces.
explanation: Each piece is the place value of one digit.
Adding the pieces back gives the original number.
lessons.rule: Expanded form = sum of each digit's place value.
lessons.tip: Write the thousands piece first, then work right.

steps.text: Split each digit into its place value.
Add the pieces to rebuild the number.

lessons.title: Putting Numbers Back Together
lessons.intro: Given the expanded pieces, you can rebuild the number by adding them up.
explanation: 6,000 + 70 + 9 rebuilds to 6,079 (there are no hundreds, so that place is 0).
Watch for missing places — they become zeros.
lessons.rule: Add all the pieces to get the standard number.
lessons.tip: A missing place means a 0 in that spot.

lessons.title: Minding the Zeros
lessons.intro: Expanded form makes zeros easy to spot — a missing place simply isn't written.
explanation: 7,000 + 800 + 5 = 7,805 (the tens place is 0).
2,000 + 90 = 2,090 (hundreds and ones are 0).
Always check every place from thousands down to ones.
lessons.rule: Fill any skipped place with 0 in the final number.
lessons.tip: List all four places so you don't forget a zero.

lessons.title: Expanded Form in Words
lessons.intro: Sometimes numbers are described in words: so many thousands, hundreds, tens and ones.
explanation: 5 thousands, 3 hundreds, 0 tens, 7 ones = 5,307.
8 thousands and 6 ones only = 8,006.
Each described group is a place value piece.
lessons.rule: Turn each spoken group into its place value, then add.
lessons.tip: Zero groups still need a 0 place-holder.

lessons.title: Tricky Expanded Sums
lessons.intro: What if a piece is bigger than its place allows? You simply carry over, just like in addition.
explanation: The 15 tens became 150, adding into the hundreds place.
Expanded form still works — just add carefully.
lessons.rule: Pieces can be any size; just add them honestly.
lessons.tip: Convert each piece to a plain number, then total.

quiz.question: What is 6,000 + 70 + 9?
quiz.hint: There are no hundreds, so that place is 0.

quiz.question: What is 2,000 + 90?
A number is made of 5 thousands, 3 hundreds, 0 tens and 7 ones. What is it?
quiz.story: Aarav builds a number from blocks.

quiz.question: A number has 8 thousands and 6 ones only. What is the number?
quiz.story: Only two place values are filled.

quiz.question: If a number equals 6 thousands + 15 tens, what is the number?

lessons.title: Which is Bigger?
lessons.intro: To compare numbers, line them up and look at the leftmost digit that is different.
explanation: 4,532 vs 4,523: thousands and hundreds match, tens differ (3 vs 2), so 4,532 is greater.
Compare place by place from the left.
The first place where they differ decides the winner.
lessons.rule: Compare from the highest place; the first difference wins.
lessons.tip: If digit counts differ, the longer number is bigger.

steps.text: Line the numbers up by place.

lessons.title: Smaller and Smallest
lessons.intro: Finding the smallest works the same way — the first differing digit, but you pick the lower one.
explanation: 7,089 vs 7,098: tens differ (8 vs 9), so 7,089 is smaller.
Among 5,600; 5,060; 5,006 the smallest is 5,006.
Always start comparing from the left.
lessons.rule: Smallest number has the lowest digit at the first difference.
lessons.tip: Scan left to right and stop at the first gap.

lessons.title: Ordering Numbers
lessons.intro: Putting several numbers in order (ascending or descending) is just comparing them in a row.
explanation: Ascending means smallest to largest; descending means largest to smallest.
Among 2,341; 2,314; 2,431 the greatest is 2,431.
Sort by the first differing place.
lessons.rule: Ascending = low to high; descending = high to low.
lessons.tip: Find the biggest, then the next, and so on.

lessons.title: Real-Life Comparisons
lessons.intro: We compare numbers every day — scores, prices, distances and more.
explanation: Scores 3,450, 3,540, 3,405: the highest is 3,540.
Prices 1,299, 1,099, 1,199: the lowest is 1,099.
Comparing helps us make smart choices.
lessons.rule: The same left-to-right rule works for money and scores.
lessons.tip: Ignore the currency sign and compare the numbers.

lessons.title: Numbers In Between
lessons.intro: Between two numbers there can be several whole numbers — counting them is a fun puzzle.
explanation: Between 2,998 and 3,002 the whole numbers are 2,999, 3,000, 3,001.
That is 3 numbers strictly in between.
Count carefully and do not include the end numbers.
lessons.rule: Count only the numbers strictly between the two ends.
lessons.tip: List them out if you are unsure.

quiz.question: Which is greater: 4,532 or 4,523? Write the greater number.
Which is smaller: 7,089 or 7,098? Write the smaller number.
Write the greatest of 2,341; 2,314; 2,431.
Write the smallest of 5,600; 5,060; 5,006.
Three friends scored 3,450, 3,540 and 3,405. What is the highest score?
quiz.story: A big day at the quiz contest!

quiz.question: Prices are 1,299, 1,099 and 1,199 rupees. What is the lowest price in rupees?
How many whole numbers lie strictly between 2,998 and 3,002?
What is the greatest 4-digit number less than 5,000 using the digits 4, 9, 8, 7 each once?
quiz.hint: It must start with 4 to stay under 5,000; arrange the rest biggest first.

lessons.title: Rounding to the Nearest Ten
lessons.intro: Rounding makes numbers simpler by snapping them to a nearby round number.
explanation: Look at the digit just to the right of the place you are rounding to.
If it is 5 or more, round up; if it is 4 or less, round down.
4,489 rounded to the nearest ten is 4,490.
lessons.rule: 5 or more rounds up; 4 or less rounds down.
lessons.tip: Only the next digit to the right decides.

steps.text: To round to tens, look at the ones digit.
Ones digit 9 is 5-or-more, so round up.
steps.tip: Up means add to the tens place.

lessons.title: Rounding to the Nearest Hundred
lessons.intro: Same rule, bigger step — now we snap to the nearest hundred.
explanation: Look at the tens digit to decide.
3,472 rounded to the nearest hundred is 3,500.
2,350 rounded to the nearest hundred is 2,400 (5 rounds up).
lessons.rule: Check the tens digit to round to hundreds.
lessons.tip: At exactly 50, always round up.

lessons.title: Rounding to the Nearest Thousand
lessons.intro: For big numbers we often round to the nearest thousand to make them easy to say.
explanation: Look at the hundreds digit to decide.
6,814 rounded to the nearest thousand is 7,000.
48,500 rounded to the nearest thousand is 49,000.
lessons.rule: Check the hundreds digit to round to thousands.
lessons.tip: Keep the chosen place and zero out everything to its right.

lessons.title: Rounding to Report
lessons.intro: Shops, towns and reports often use rounded numbers because they are easier to remember.
explanation: A shop that sold 2,780 items reports about 2,800.
Rounded numbers are approximate, not exact.
We use the word 'about' to show it is rounded.
lessons.rule: Rounded numbers are approximate — say 'about'.
lessons.tip: Round to whatever place the report needs.

lessons.title: Estimating Answers
lessons.intro: Before calculating, estimate by rounding each number — it tells you roughly what to expect.
explanation: Estimates help you check if your exact answer is sensible.
lessons.rule: Round each number first, then add or subtract.
lessons.tip: Use estimation to catch big mistakes.

quiz.question: Round 3,472 to the nearest hundred.
Round 6,814 to the nearest thousand.
Round 2,350 to the nearest hundred.
quiz.hint: The tens digit is 5, so round up.

quiz.question: Round 4,489 to the nearest ten.
A shop sold 2,780 items. Round this to the nearest hundred for the report.
quiz.hint: The tens digit is 8, so round up.
quiz.story: Time for the weekly sales report.

quiz.question: A town has 48,500 people. Round this to the nearest thousand.
quiz.hint: The hundreds digit is 5, so round up.
quiz.story: The census team needs a round figure.

quiz.question: Estimate 412 + 289 by rounding each to the nearest hundred, then adding.
Estimate 6,120 - 2,970 by rounding each to the nearest thousand, then subtracting.
